source.title: Transcoders Trace Visual Grounding and Hallucinations in Vision-Language Models
source.authors: Dimitrios Damianos; Leon Voukoutis; G. Skyrianos; Vassilis Katsouros; Georgios Paraskevopoulos

record.tranche_reason: The paper reports monosemanticity-related measurements for transcoder features, not neuron poles or neuron explanations; it does not test any listed claim version.
record.gate_note: The paper's feature-sharing results are recorded as related findings, not tests of neuron interpretability. Its attribution, patch-ablation, circuit-tracing, and hallucination-classification results do not measure the neuron claims in the versions.
record.test_reason: The study trains transcoders and SAEs on Gemma 3-4B-IT and reports patch-ablation, circuit-tracing and hallucination-classification results plus a transcoder-feature token-sharing count. None of these audits the model's own neurons, compares neuron interpretability across models, analyses InceptionV1, tests neurons as circuit units, or scores neuron explanations. The monosemanticity analysis concerns trained transcoder features and uses token-sharing, not explanation quality.
record.authors_conclusion: Largely correct. The authors' main conclusion is that transcoder (function-centric) decomposition gives more faithful attributions than SAEs for visually grounded tokens in Gemma 3-4B-IT. Its circuit traces also give a modest hallucination signal (AUC 0.68). On monosemanticity, the authors say extracted features 'are not monosemantic' and that representation is distributed, while defending the approach.
record.recipe_differences: The paper trains transcoder and SAE decompositions of Gemma 3-4B-IT MLP computation and analyzes their features; it does not use the neuron-pole audit method.

fits_no_version.finding: Only 4 of 40,960 transcoder features (0.01%) activate for a single token. 51.4% are shared by 21–100 tokens, and 45 fire for all 2,413 tokens (Table 5).
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: In Gemma 3-4B-IT, transcoder features trained on MLP outputs are mostly shared across many tokens rather than token-specific.

fits_no_version.finding: Rare tokens (fewer than 20 occurrences) activate an average of 49.4 transcoder features per layer, versus 35.4 for high-frequency tokens.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Rare tokens recruit more transcoder features per layer than frequent tokens.

record.code_released: Code, trained Transcoders, and datasets are promised upon acceptance; URL not stated.
record.problems: The feature-sharing analysis concerns transcoder features rather than neurons, and the paper notes that the analysis uses 10,000 Flickr30K samples. No uncertainty estimates are given for these feature-sharing results.
record.rows_left_out: No claim-relevant neuron results were reported. Other results on attribution and patch ablation, false visual grounding, circuit traces, and hallucination classification were left out because they do not measure the listed neuron claims.

untested.parts: No neuron interpretability shares across models or scale. Only Gemma 3-4B-IT, and only via transcoders.
No InceptionV1 or canonical polysemantic neuron analysis.
No test of architecture, regularization or tools as causes of neuron interpretability.
Circuits are built from trained transcoders, i.e. a replacement model. Neurons are not tested as circuit units.
No held-out test of explanations from activating examples.
No simulation-based scoring of neuron explanations.

record.verdict_notes: Token-sharing count is a weak proxy for monosemanticity: a feature firing on many tokens may still encode one concept. It also bears on trained features, not raw neurons, so it cannot speak to V1, V2 or V7 even indirectly. Not an original source.

versions.untested_parts: No Qwen3-32B neuron-pole audit or estimate of poles with one or two jobs or not understood.
No comparison of neuron-pole interpretability across models, architectures, or scale.
No InceptionV1 cat-and-car neuron analysis or test of recursive generalization versus superposition.
No test of architecture, regularization, or tools as causes of neuron interpretability rates.
The paper uses transcoders for circuit tracing; it does not test whether a model's own neurons suffice as circuit units or compare against a trained replacement model.
No test of explanations against activations beyond the examples used to write them.
No automated scoring of neuron explanations by predicting activations on new text.

rows.subject: Gemma 3-4B-IT
rows.operation_detail: Counted transcoder features by how many distinct tokens they were shared across.
rows.measure: Number and percentage of features in token-sharing category
rows.note: Feature-sharing counts are reported across the corpus; this measures transcoder features, not neurons.
rows.check: Transcoder feature count, not a neuron measure. 'Observed' has no version effect to refer to. Token-sharing count does not measure whether a unit has one coherent job.
